14860-the-journal-of-sir-walter-scott-fr:
Sir Walter Scott's journal, from the original manuscript at Abbotsford, opens volume one with a motto. It urges working while it is day, for the night comes when no man can work. Scott placed that text on his dial stone years before, and it often preached in vain.

Entries follow his daily round. A peep at Bothwell Castle for half an hour recalls many memories, and Scott reflects on how changed he is from the young man passionately ambitious of fame. The journal, first published in 1890, shows a working writer managing debts, books and visitors. It is intimate, unguarded and full of the business of a literary life.
15663-ancient-egypt:
A history of ancient Egypt by George Rawlinson, Camden Professor of Ancient History at Oxford, with Arthur Gilman as collaborator. First issued in London in 1886, it moves from the land itself through kings, faith, and daily life. Rawlinson draws on monuments, tombs, and Greek writers to build a full survey. The tenth edition shows a book that schools and general readers used for decades.

Chapters cover the Nile valley, the pyramids, the great temples at Karnak, and the long line of rulers. Religion, law, art, and trade each get careful treatment, with dates tied to monuments where possible. Rawlinson keeps the focus on what the stones and texts can prove. The result still works as a firm, readable guide to a civilisation that lasted for thousands of years.
15721-the-hawk-of-egypt:
A desert romance by Joan Conquest, author of Desert Love, issued by the Macaulay Company in New York in 1922. Conquest sets her tale in Egypt, among tents, sheikhs, and desert law. A girl stands trembling before a tent no foot but his has trod, as the frontispiece shows. The novel promises passion, danger, and the clash of East and West.

The Hawk, a proud desert chief, claims love with the same force he claims rule. An English girl must weigh freedom against a fierce, tender captor. Arabic words and desert custom colour every scene. Conquest writes for readers who liked strong romance in strange lands: swift, warm, and full of desert colour, with love as the prize of the contest.
17816-letters-from-egypt:
Lady Duff Gordon's letters from Egypt appear here in a revised edition. It carries a memoir by her daughter Janet Ross and a new introduction by George Meredith. A second impression was published in London in 1902 by R. Brimley Johnson. A photograph from a sketch by G. F. Watts, about 1848, fronts the volume. Ross's memoir opens the book.

Lucie Duff Gordon, born June 24, 1821, was the only child of John and Sarah Austin, inheriting their beauty and intellect. Her letters from Egypt, written in illness and exile, made her famous as an observer of Egyptian life. Readers get a classic of travel letters, warm, sharp, and humane.
18647-peeps-at-many-lands-egypt:
R. Talbot Kelly wrote this children's travel book on Egypt at London in 1916 with Adam and Charles Black, with twelve color pictures by the author. Chapters cover antiquity, the land, Cairo in two parts, the Nile in three parts, the monuments, the people, and the desert. A sketch map and views of mosques, the first cataract, the pyramids of Gizeh, and desert Arabs aid the text.

Kelly opens with Joseph, the shepherd boy sold into Egypt who rose to rule, to frame the land's long past. Temples, tombs, and hieroglyphs still record those Bible times, he notes. The book gives young readers a vivid, picture-led tour of Egypt.
19715-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
C. H. B. Quennell wrote this guide to Norwich Cathedral for Bell's cathedral series, published in London in the late eighteen hundreds with forty pictures. It gives the fabric's history, a walk round the outside, and a tour of the inside, with a history of the East Anglian bishops and a chapter on the city.

Bay by bay, the guide reads the carvings: Christ among the doctors, the marriage at Cana, the raising of Lazarus, the Last Supper, and the washing of feet. Made for visitors, it still serves as a clear companion to a great Norman church.
19804-three-centuries-of-a-city-library-:
Norwich holds a rare place in library history, writes Geo. A. Stephen. Its city library dates to 1608. The present public library opened in 1857. Stephen's title promises three centuries of that story. Norwich claims one of England's earliest provincial public libraries. It was also first to adopt the Public Libraries Act of 1850.

Stephen hoped local readers and archaeologists would use his sketch. A library's history mirrors its city's civic pride. Norwich's 1608 foundation predates most public collections. The 1850 act let towns fund libraries from local rates. Norwich led, and Stephen documents the lead. Library historians still start English public provision with cities like this.
2131-an-account-of-egypt:
Herodotus, translated by G. C. Macaulay, gives his account of Egypt, drawn from travel down the Nile and talk with priests and guides. Born at Halicarnassus in the early fifth century before Christ, he gathered his history by journeying. Macaulay's translation, made in the nineteenth century, keeps Herodotus readable for students.

Egypt's river, temples, customs, and kings fill this section of his great work on Greeks and barbarians, which runs to the battle of Mycale in 479 before Christ. Herodotus mixes wonder, doubt, and story, and his Egypt still reads as a traveller's tale. Egypt's Nile, with its floods and temples, fascinated Greek travellers as it fascinates readers now.
22224-at-aboukir-and-acre-a-story-of-nap:
G. A. Henty told Napoleon's invasion of Egypt in At Aboukir and Acre. Henty's boy hero serves through the campaign of 1798 and 1799. At Aboukir, Nelson destroyed the French fleet; at Acre, Sir Sidney Smith stopped Napoleon himself. Henty opens among the guns of a captured fort, clean and ready only because the dry climate keeps rust away.

Battles by land and sea, marches, and sieges fill the tale. The hero carries messages, escapes Turks and Frenchmen, and watches great men at work. Henty aimed to teach history through adventure, and his facts are carefully placed. Few books are more typical of Henty: brisk, imperial, and stuffed with the real campaign.
22799-peeps-at-many-lands-ancient-egypt:
The Rev. James Baikie wrote Ancient Egypt in the Peeps at Many Lands series, short, illustrated country books for young readers. The catalog record gives no year. Baikie, a Scottish minister and keen Egyptologist, introduces the land of the Nile to children who may know it first from Bible stories.

Asked to name the world's most interesting country, he begins, most people would say Palestine. Not for anything wonderful in the land itself, they would add. The reason is all the great things that happened there, above all its being the home of our Lord. Against that favorite he sets Egypt's claim: pharaohs, pyramids, and the Exodus itself. The Peeps volumes mixed geography, history, and daily life in a hundred pages. Baikie's Egypt is a friendly first expedition.
22880-bell-s-cathedrals-a-short-account-:
The Reverend T. Perkins guides readers through Romsey Abbey in this volume of Bell's Cathedrals. Records before the abbey's first foundation simply do not exist, he admits, nor for many years after. Florence of Worcester supplies the earliest firm reference. His chronicle, which mentions the abbey under the year 967, predates his own death in 1118.

From that early convent of Saints Mary and Ethelfleda, Perkins traces the great Norman church that still stands in Hampshire. Architecture, abbesses, and local legend share the pages in the series' usual blend. The book was made for travelers who wanted solid fact in a small format. Its care with sources, even while confessing gaps, gives it lasting use.
23994-there-was-a-king-in-egypt:
Norma Lorimer, author of By the Waters of Germany and A Wife Out of Egypt, published There Was a King in Egypt in London in 1918. It opens at dawn, in stillness among barren hills and soft sands, where only an Englishman stirs, standing at his tent door.

At sunrise and sunset, Lorimer writes, the East is its own, and every suggestion of Western influence is wiped out. The land of the Pharaohs, kingdom of Ra the sun god whose cradle was at Heliopolis, returns to the days when the sun governed religion. The Nile, mother of life, had not yet hidden the infant Moses among her reeds. Each dawn sees Michael Amory, wrapped in his thickest coat, waiting for Ra above the desert horizon.
28001-inaugural-presidential-address-off:
This volume contains President Barack Obama's two inaugural addresses, of January 20, 2009, and January 21, 2013, in the official transcript as prepared for delivery and released by the Presidential Inaugural Committee. The first address opens with Obama humbled by the task, grateful for trust, and mindful of sacrifices borne by ancestors.

Obama thanks President Bush for service and cooperation, notes that forty-four Americans have taken the oath, and warns that homes have been lost, jobs shed, and businesses shuttered. The volume preserves both addresses as delivered, companion to the volunteer transcriptions in the companion e-book.
28698-the-crystal-crypt:
Philip K. Dick's The Crystal Crypt opens on the last Inner-Flight ship leaving Mars for Terra. Told to put down at the Deimos control station for inspection, the ship settles under the watch of three slender Martian pursuit craft. Passengers glance uneasily at the small speck of rock below, the final checkpoint before war.

These Terrans, businessmen, expatriates, and tourists, are the last to leave the grim red planet, and talk turns to whether Mars will dare fight. One woman, three years on Mars, warns that Mars is desperate and will fight tooth and nail. Armed Martian soldiers soon cross the field at double time. Readers get a tense Cold War tale, set between worlds.
29010-the-religion-of-ancient-egypt:
W. M. Flinders Petrie wrote this 1906 book, The Religion of Ancient Egypt, published by Archibald Constable in London. Petrie, Edwards professor of Egyptology at University College, London, treats the nature of gods and of man, the future life, and animal worship. Later chapters cover groups of gods, animal-headed, human, cosmic, abstract, and foreign, with the cosmogony, ritual and priesthood, and sacred books.

The book closes with private worship, Egyptian ethics, and the influence of Egypt, with an index and a list of principal works. A frontispiece shows Egyptian gods from Petrie's own collection. Readers get a compact, authoritative survey by the greatest Egyptologist of his age, clear enough for general readers and solid enough for students.
3407-the-spell-of-egypt:
Robert Hichens writes a travel book about Egypt that moves from monument to monument along the Nile. Its chapters take in the Pyramids, the Sphinx, Sakkara, Abydos, Denderah, Karnak, Luxor, the Tombs of the Kings, Edfu, Kom Ombos, Philae, and Old Cairo. Hichens asks why people come to Egypt at all, whether to gain a dream or to recover old ones.

His answer favors atmosphere over mere facts. He credits the sun god Kheper, in Egyptian myth, with giving Egypt its inner light, while human builders supplied its marvels. The book mixes description, legend, and personal feeling, and it suits readers who want the romance of Egypt before they turn to a guidebook.
8517-hormones-and-heredity-a-discussion-:
J. T. Cunningham, a zoology teacher at East London College, wrote Hormones and Heredity in 1921, published by Constable in London. He asks how hormones, the body's chemical messengers, might shape heredity and the growth of new traits. His first part looks back at past theories of chemical sway on growth.

Cunningham wrote before modern genetics gave firm answers, when old ideas about traits gained in life still had life in them. His book shows science in flux, with a clear case made and fairly weighed. Read it as a record of 1921 biology, not as current science, and it still teaches how theories change.
8672-poems-chiefly-from-manuscript:
John Clare's poems, gathered chiefly from manuscript, bring together work chosen from more than two thousand poems considered by the editor. Over two-thirds of those examined had never been published, and ninety poems in this volume appear in print for the first time, marked with asterisks in the contents. A few more are rescued from periodicals, and many familiar poems are reset against their manuscript versions.

The arrangement follows Clare's development, including early juvenilia, so readers can watch the Northamptonshire labourer-poet grow from village verses to mature nature poetry. Clare's birds, fields, and seasons are described with a closeness few poets match. The volume matters for Clare scholars and for any reader who wants the poet beyond the famous anthology pieces, in the fuller shape his manuscripts reveal.
9799-it-happened-in-egypt:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson wrote It Happened in Egypt in 1914, a tale of adventures grave and gay on the Nile. The book opens with a secret and a girl, Cleopatra and a ship's mystery, and a man in a green turban. A dragoman, a café of Abdullahi, and the great Sir Marcus follow. Revelations from a retired colonel and Foxy Duffing deepen the plot.

Later chapters bring a house of the crocodile, a night of full moon, and a desert diary to its bitter end. The Asiut affair and a zone of fire close the chase. A reader gets a brisk Egyptian adventure, rich in ships, deserts, and secrets.
an-account-of-egypt:
Herodotus describes Egypt in the second book of his Histories, translated here by G. C. Macaulay. The prefatory note gives his life in brief: born at Halicarnassus in the early fifth century B.C., a great traveler, settled at last in Thurii, where he composed his work. Egypt drew him as the oldest land he knew.

He reports the Nile's flooding and its mystery, the customs of the Egyptians, their gods, temples, and burial rites, and the building of the pyramids. Kings' lists, priests' tales, and wonders he saw himself stand side by side. Macaulay's clear English keeps Herodotus's curious, questioning voice, the voice of the first great travel writer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-pre:
A canonical precept is a command from a church superior that binds a particular person. The entry draws a sharp line between it and a law. A law binds a whole community and outlives its maker until repealed. A precept binds named inferiors only while the giver holds office, and it ends with them. The distinction turns on who is bound, where the command reaches, and how long it lasts.

The entry then turns to discipline. A bishop warns a cleric twice after an informal inquiry. If nothing changes, he issues a written precept naming the act required or forbidden and the penalty for disobedience. If the cleric cannot be reached, the precept may be posted in public. Failure to amend can lead to a formal trial. The piece thus links a general definition to a concrete church-court procedure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-ap:
The Council of Apt, held on 14 May 1365 in Apt cathedral, gathered the archbishops and bishops of Arles, Embrun, and Aix in southern France. Twenty-eight decrees came from the meeting, a compact record of provincial church government in the fourteenth century.

Pilgrims earned eleven days of indulgence by visiting Apt's church of the Blessed Virgin on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. They came with pious sentiments to venerate relics kept there. The entry preserves the decrees' substance and the sources behind them, Mansi, Martene, and a local history of Apt's church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crypt:
An architectural entry defines the crypt, from a word meaning a hidden place, and traces its descent from early Christian burial chambers. When visits to tombs outside Rome's walls fell from use, the Church brought martyrs inside the walls, digging tombs beneath churches to hold their relics. So arose the confessio of basilicas, and later the crypt of medieval churches.

The Romanesque crypt descends directly from the hypogoeum, or underground chamber, of the catacombs. An early example stands at Sant' Apollinare in Classe at Ravenna, dated 534. Some crypts sank as deep as catacomb chambers, others rose partly above ground and took light from small side windows. The term also covers the lower storey of a two-storey building, as at the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-egypt:
Egypt is treated here in one vast survey, split into seven parts. They cover the land, ancient history, ancient religion, literary monuments, the Coptic Church, Coptic literature, and Copto-Arabic literature. The opening part bounds Egypt proper to the Nile valley from the Mediterranean to the First Cataract at Assuan. That stretch is some six hundred and eighty miles by rail. Egyptian sway reached far south into Nubia.

Readers move from the narrow valley, where farm land is often only a few hundred yards wide. They pass the cataract and its great dam. Then they follow the long story of kings and gods, and on to the Christian Egypt of the Copts and their books. No single short entry could hold so much, and this one is best used as a map: find the division you need, then follow its own full account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-islam-concept:
Islam, an Arabic word that since Muhammad's time names the religion of Muhammad and the Koran, is unpacked here from its grammar outward. The root salima means to be safe or secure. Its second form means to make someone safe or free. Its third means to make peace or be reconciled. Its fourth, aslama, means to resign, submit, or surrender. Islam is the infinitive of that fourth form.

In its religious sense, then, Islam means the entire surrender of the will to God. Christianity likewise names the religion of Jesus and the Gospels. Judaism names that of Moses, the prophets, and the Old Testament. Those who so surrender are called Muslimun, singular Muslim, from the participle form. The entry gives readers the word's build before its creed, so the name itself explains the faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plagues-of-eg:
The Plagues of Egypt were the ten calamities sent on Egypt to break Pharaoh's refusal to free the Israelites. Moses' demand only worsened the people's lot, and Aaron's rod turned serpent failed to move Pharaoh, since Egyptian magicians copied the wonder. A chain of afflictions followed, ending in the death of Egypt's first-born.

Seven plagues came through Moses and Aaron and three, the fourth, fifth, and tenth, by God's direct action, the entry explains. The last four fell in quick succession between early March and early April, when barley was in ear and flax in bud. The entry describes the first plague, the Nile turned to blood, and weighs whether the water truly changed or merely took the river's reddish flood colour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-mary-of:
Mary of Egypt, born probably about 344 and dead about 421, anchors one of the most famous conversion stories of the early desert saints. At twelve she ran away to Alexandria, where she lived for over seventeen years as a prostitute. Her entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia retells the legend that turned a life of excess into a model of repentance.

Sailing to Jerusalem for the feast of the Holy Cross, she found herself barred from the church by some unseen force, and remorse broke over her in the churchyard. She crossed the Jordan and spent the rest of her life alone in the desert in penance. The entry presents the tale as tradition rather than documented history, and shows how it became a favourite Lenten reading.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-transept:
A transept is a rectangular space set between apse and nave in the early Christian basilica. It arose from the need for room for more clergy and for proper celebration of the service. Its length may equal the full breadth of the nave, as at Santa Maria Maggiore and Santa Croce in Rome, or stretch beyond the nave walls on either side.

Long thought peculiar to the Roman basilica, the transept also appears in Asia Minor churches such as Sagalassos. In a second early form, found in Asia Minor and Sicily, the transept grows organically from the whole structure into a cross-shaped church. Three squares match the nave in height and breadth, a fourth forms the choir, and the apse beyond completes the cross. Most transepts end in straight north and south walls, though German churches vary the pattern.
doe-osti-3011809-commercialization-of-a-: Heliostat errors got optically measured, and this DOE text commercializes NIO technology. The pages detail the utility findings. The solar folks get their data. The technology was non-intrusive optical. The data were solar. The errors were optical. The scale was utility.
doe-osti-3020691-hydrogen-infrastructure: Hydrogen could power trucks and factories with no exhaust but water — if the fueling network existed. This report models how to build that network: where to make hydrogen, how to move it, and what it costs. The math helps planners avoid billion-dollar mistakes before breaking ground.
doe-osti-3030179-investigating-extracell: Electron uptake got extracellularly investigated, and this DOE text studies redox substrates. The pages detail the mechanism findings. The bio folks get their data. The substrates were solid. The data were bio. The active were redox. The mechanisms were gaining.
doe-osti-3375597-outline-for-preliminary: AI got air-quality-outlined, and this DOE outline covers community proof. The pages detail the preliminary findings. The environmental folks get their data. The concept was preliminary. The data were environmental. The quality were air. The community were proof.
freytag-the-lost-manuscript:
Scholars hunt a precious lost manuscript, and their own lives tangle into the search, in Gustav Freytag's The Lost Manuscript, presented here in English. A German university town supplies the scene: professors, rivals, and families orbiting one missing bundle of old Latin prose. The hunt gives the comedy its engine.

Affectionate satire of the academic world fills the book, from a novelist who knew professors well. Love plots and scholarly feuds intertwine until the manuscript hunt mirrors the hunt for happiness. A serious heart beats under the comedy of learning. Freytag writes professors as people first and pedants second, mostly. English readers will find the novel charming, intelligent, and quietly wise about ambition.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_USCYB:
In 2010, WikiLeaks published a huge trove of State Department cables, an episode known as Cable-Gate. A decade later, in March 2020, the National Security Archive reported on a United States Cyber Command review. It assessed what that leak had cost American cyber defenses. The review was released in answer to the Archive's own Freedom of Information Act request.

A USCYBERCOM Fusion Cell judged that material in the cables had revealed American intelligence on adversary cyber operations. In plain terms, diplomatic gossip carried operational secrets, and foreign hackers, the kind tracked as APT groups, gained from reading them. The situational awareness report at the center of the posting lets readers see a leak's damage assessed by the very command charged with fighting the intrusions it may have aided.
letters-from-egypt:
Lucie Duff Gordon's Letters from Egypt appear here with a memoir by George Meredith. R. Brimley Johnson issued this second impression in London in 1902. A Watts sketch of the author serves as frontispiece.

The memoir notes she was born on June 24, 1821. Her father, John Austin, wrote on the philosophy of law. Duff Gordon traveled to Egypt for her health and stayed for years. Her letters describe Egyptian people with rare warmth and respect. They remain among the finest English letters from the Nile. Her move up the Nile to Luxor deepens the letters. Illness never dulled her eye for character and custom.
peeps-at-many-lands-egypt: The hosted sample here shows only the front matter of Peeps at Many Lands: Egypt, the title page and start of the contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names R. Talbot Kelly as author and illustrator of twelve full-page colour pictures, published in London by Adam and Charles Black in 1916. The contents begin with Egypt's antiquity and the land itself, then move to two chapters on Cairo and two on the Nile.
poems-chiefly-from-manuscript:
John Clare, the Northamptonshire peasant poet, left behind thousands of poems, and Poems Chiefly from Manuscript draws its selection from that store. An editor's note explains the scale of the task: over two thousand poems were considered and compared. More than two thirds of them unpublished, and ninety pieces in the volume are printed for the first time. Poems Clare published in periodicals and manuscripts kept at the Peterborough Museum both fed the selection.

Arrangement is chronological where dates can be guessed from handwriting and style, with some early juvenilia and some of the Asylum Poems Clare wrote during his years in mental asylums. Editors supplied punctuation, which Clare cheerfully left to others, and restored stanzas earlier editors had dropped. The book is a rescue operation, recovering a major nature poet from his own scattered papers.
the-hawk-of-egypt: Joan Conquest wrote The Hawk of Egypt, published in New York by The Macaulay Company with a 1922 copyright, and a frontispiece by G. W. Gage. Conquest is named as the author of Desert Love and Leonie of the Jungle, and a note states that all names in the book are fictitious. Only the title pages, a dedication, and the first line of chapter one are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
the-journal-of-sir-walter-scott-from-the: Sir Walter Scott's journal is printed here from the Abbotsford manuscript, in the Burt Franklin reprint of 1970; first publication came in 1890. The front pages carry Scott's motto from his dial-stone. I must work while it is called day, for the night cometh when no man can work. He admits it often preached in vain. Only the title pages and a letter extract are present here. The journal entries themselves do not appear. The extract has Scott writing to Lord Montagu in June 1825 about Bothwell Castle.
the-spell-of-egypt: Robert Hichens wrote this Egyptian travel book, prepared here from a 1911 edition published by the Century Company of New York. The pages present here give the title page, the preparer's note, and a contents list of seventeen numbered chapters without titles, so the travel chapters themselves do not appear. A companion record under a longer file name carries the same book with titled chapters and its opening pages.
